summary:
Allwork.Space marks International Coworking Day (August 9, 2026) with a curated list of must-read articles for flexible workspace operators, presented in themed sections. The framing argues flexible workspaces will play a more critical role in the future of work, touching digital transformation, remote work, sustainability and inclusivity.

Section one, understanding the state of the industry: (1) A coworking statistics and trends guide covering adoption, market size, regional growth, pricing, profitability and trends through 2030, and the sector's shift from a freelancer/startup solution to a component of corporate real estate strategy. (2) An exclusive on WeWork CEO John Santora's Global Workspace Association Conference keynote, where he said the industry is not adding space fast enough to meet demand while cautioning against expansion without a clear path to profitability; his seven takeaways span demand validation, sustainable deals, collaboration with competitors, technology and workplace culture. (3) IWG's 2026 midyear update, reporting record system-wide revenue and a leadership transition as founder Mark Dixon steps aside after nearly four decades, with the capital-light managed and franchised division outgrowing the wider company, illustrating the sector's move away from capital-intensive leases toward management agreements, franchising and recurring fees. (4) An explainer on new U.K. business rates, warning that flexible workspace buildings previously split into separately assessed offices may be treated as a single rateable property, exposing operators to rates on entire centers including vacant space, with higher multipliers for larger properties adding margin pressure.

Section two, increasing revenue and visibility: (5) Google Reviews guidance, noting revised Google policies and AI-powered enforcement can delete reviews or suspend Business Profiles, including for requesting reviews while customers are still on site. (6) Part-time private office memberships as an underused product, letting operators sell multiple recurring memberships against the same room because members rarely use all available hours. The excerpt cuts off mid-item.
